questions.stem: What size range defines a nanoparticle?
questions.explanation: Nanoparticles are defined as particles with dimensions between 1 and 100 nanometres (nm). A nanometre is one billionth of a metre (10⁻⁹ m). This is roughly the scale of individual molecules and small clusters of atoms. Fine particles are larger (100 nm - 0.01 mm) and coarse particles are larger still.

questions.stem: Why do nanoparticles of silver have stronger antibacterial properties than a solid lump of silver of the same mass?

options.text: Nanoparticles contain a different type of silver
Nanoparticles have a much higher surface area to volume ratio, so more silver atoms can interact with bacteria
Nanoparticles are lighter than bulk silver
Nanoparticles dissolve in water but bulk silver does not

questions.explanation: When a material is divided into nanoparticles, the total surface area increases dramatically while the total volume stays the same. This high surface area to volume ratio means many more silver atoms are exposed at the surface and can interact with bacteria. The silver atoms themselves are identical to those in bulk silver.

questions.stem: A cube with sides of 1 cm is cut into cubes with sides of 1 nm. What happens to the total surface area?
questions.explanation: When a large cube is divided into many tiny cubes, new surfaces are created with each cut. The total volume remains the same, but the total surface area increases enormously. Dividing a 1 cm cube into 1 nm cubes would increase the surface area by a factor of about 10 million. This is why nanoparticles have such a high surface area to volume ratio.

questions.stem: Titanium dioxide nanoparticles are used in sunscreen. Why might there be concerns about using nanoparticles in consumer products?

options.text: Nanoparticles are too expensive to produce
Their small size means they could enter cells and have unknown long-term health effects
They make the sunscreen less effective

questions.explanation: Due to their extremely small size, nanoparticles can potentially penetrate cell membranes and enter the body in ways that larger particles cannot. The long-term health and environmental effects of nanoparticles are not yet fully understood. This is why there is ongoing research and debate about the safety of nanoparticles in consumer products.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a use of nanoparticles?

options.text: As catalysts in industrial processes due to high surface area

questions.explanation: Nanoparticles are used as catalysts because their very high surface area to volume ratio provides many active sites for reactions, making them much more effective than bulk materials. They are also used in medicine (drug delivery), electronics (computer components), cosmetics (sunscreen), and coatings (self-cleaning surfaces).
